content: This updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2015, investigates the potential role of yoga as a therapeutic intervention for epilepsy. Yoga is hypothesized to promote relaxation, reduce stress, and modulate the autonomic nervous system and electroencephalographic activity, which may contribute to seizure control. If proven effective, yoga could serve as an appealing non-pharmacological treatment option for epilepsy. The primary objectives of this review were to determine whether individuals with epilepsy who practice yoga are more likely to achieve seizure freedom, experience a significant reduction in seizure frequency or duration, or report an improved quality of life. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, SCOPUS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to January 3, 2017. Additional searches included registries from the Yoga Biomedical Trust and the Research Council for Complementary Medicine. No language restrictions were applied. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults with uncontrolled epilepsy, comparing yoga to either no treatment or other behavioral interventions. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion and extracted data. The outcomes evaluated included the percentage of participants achieving seizure freedom, changes in seizure frequency and duration, and quality of life. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated for the outcomes. No new studies were identified for this update, leaving the results unchanged from the previous review. The earlier review included two unblinded RCTs involving 50 participants with refractory epilepsy. Of these, 18 participants were assigned to yoga, while 32 were allocated to control interventions. All participants continued their antiepileptic drug regimens. The baseline phase lasted three months, and the treatment phase ranged from five weeks to six months. Randomization methods included a die roll in one study and a computerized randomization table in the other, but neither study adequately described allocation concealment, leading to an unclear risk of bias. Overall, the studies were rated as having a low risk of bias, as all participants were included in the analysis, all expected outcomes were reported, and no other sources of bias were identified. The pooled results from the two studies showed the following: 1. Seizure freedom for six months: Yoga vs. sham yoga: OR 14.54 (95% CI 0.67 to 316.69). Yoga vs. no treatment: OR 17.31 (95% CI 0.80 to 373.45). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) vs. yoga: OR 1.00 (95% CI 0.16 to 6.42). 2. Reduction in seizure frequency: Yoga vs. sham yoga: Mean difference −2.10 (95% CI −3.15 to −1.05). Yoga vs. no treatment: Mean difference −1.10 (95% CI −1.80 to −0.40). 3. More than 50% reduction in seizure frequency: Yoga vs. sham yoga: OR 81.00 (95% CI 4.36 to 1504.46). Yoga vs. no treatment: OR 158.33 (95% CI 5.78 to 4335.63). ACT vs. yoga: OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.04 to 14.75). 4. More than 50% reduction in seizure duration: Yoga vs. sham yoga: OR 45.00 (95% CI 2.01 to 1006.75). Yoga vs. no treatment: OR 53.57 (95% CI 2.42 to 1187.26). ACT vs. yoga: OR 0.67 (95% CI 0.10 to 4.35). In one study (Panjwani 1996), no statistically significant differences were observed between the three groups in terms of seizure outcomes. Additionally, the duration of epilepsy was not comparable across groups. No data on quality of life were reported in this study. In the other study (Lundgren 2008), no significant differences were found between the yoga and ACT groups regarding seizure-free rates, a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, or seizure duration at one-year follow-up. However, the yoga group demonstrated significant improvement in quality of life as measured by the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS) (P < 0.05), while the ACT group showed significant improvement on the WHO Quality of Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF) scale (P < 0.01). The overall quality of evidence was assessed as low, and no reliable conclusions can currently be drawn regarding the efficacy of yoga as a treatment for epilepsy. Methodological limitations, including the small number of studies, limited sample sizes, lack of blinding, and insufficient data on quality-of-life outcomes, hinder the ability to make definitive recommendations. Further high-quality research is necessary to evaluate the potential benefits of yoga for refractory epilepsy. In conclusion, while the limited evidence suggests a possible beneficial effect of yoga in seizure control, the findings are inconclusive due to the low quality of the available data. Future studies should address these methodological shortcomings to provide more robust evidence on the role of yoga in managing epilepsy.
